new_note: *Up then, and eat bread, and forsake us not, as the shepherd that leaveth his flock in the hands of cruel wolves.* (2 Esdras 5:18). *So when they had dined, Yahusha (Jesus) saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Adonai (Lord); thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs.* (John 21:15). Phaltiel the captain finds Ezra fasting in the field and begs him not to leave the people the way a shepherd leaves his flock to the wolves, because Yashar'el (Israel) in the land of their captivity had been committed to him. The risen Yahusha (Jesus) sets bread before Peter and then asks him three times whether he loves him, once for each denial, and every answer comes back as a charge to feed the flock. Peter had forsaken his Master on the night of the trial; now he is told plainly what love looks like in a shepherd: eat the bread set before you, and do not leave the lambs to the wolves. The picture Phaltiel used as a warning is the very failure the threefold charge turns around.
member_note: 2 Esdras 5:18 — *forsake us not, as the shepherd that leaveth his flock in the hands of cruel wolves.* Peter, who forsook three times, is charged three times to feed the flock (John 21:15).

new_note: *And said, O Yahuah (God) that bearest rule, of every wood of the earth, and of all the trees thereof, you have chosen you one only vine:* (2 Esdras 5:23). *For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.* (Matthew 20:1). Ezra, praying, names what the Most High did with the whole earth: out of every wood and every tree he chose one vine. When Yahusha (Jesus) opens the parable of the labourers, the householder's vineyard is not a new field; it is that one vine, the vineyard Isaiah had already named as the house of Yashar'el (Israel) (Isaiah 5:7). Labourers are hired into it at different hours, but the vineyard itself was chosen long before the morning began. Whoever is brought in at the eleventh hour is brought into that same vineyard, not into a different one planted beside it.
member_note: 2 Esdras 5:23 — *of every wood of the earth, and of all the trees thereof, you have chosen you one only vine.* The householder's vineyard at Matthew 20:1 is that one chosen vine, and the labourers are hired into it.

new_note: *And said, O Yahuah (God) that bearest rule, of every wood of the earth, and of all the trees thereof, you have chosen you one only vine:* (2 Esdras 5:23). *And he began to speak unto them by parables. A certain man planted a vineyard, and set an hedge about it, and digged a place for the winefat, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country.* (Mark 12:1). The vineyard of the parable is not a figure Yahusha (Jesus) invents on the spot; Ezra had already prayed it back to the Most High, who out of all the trees of the earth chose one only vine. In the parable that chosen vine is hedged, given a winefat and a tower, and let out to husbandmen while the owner goes into a far country. Everything the husbandmen later do, they do to a vineyard that was never theirs. The one vine remains the owner's choice; the keepers were only ever entrusted with it.
member_note: 2 Esdras 5:23 — *you have chosen you one only vine.* The vineyard let out to husbandmen at Mark 12:1 was the owner's choice, never the keepers'.

new_note: *And of all lands of the whole world you have chosen you one pit: and of all the flowers thereof one lily:* (2 Esdras 5:24). *He shall come and destroy these husbandmen, and shall give the vineyard to others. And when they heard it, they said, Elohim (God) forbid.* (Luke 20:16). Ezra's prayer counts the Most High's choices one by one: one vine, one pit, one lily, one river, one city, one dove, one sheep, and at last one people (2 Esdras 5:23–27). When the parable ends with the vineyard given to others, those who heard it cried out against it, as though the chosen vine itself were being handed to a different people. But it is the husbandmen who are destroyed, not the vineyard. What passes to others is the keeping of the one vine; the vine the Most High chose out of all the lands of the whole world remains the one he chose.
member_note: 2 Esdras 5:24 — *of all lands of the whole world you have chosen you one pit.* At Luke 20:16 the keeping passes to others; the chosen vine stays the Most High's own.

new_note: *And among all the multitudes of people you have gotten you one people: and to this people, whom you lovedst, you gavest a law that is approved of all.* (2 Esdras 5:27). *What shall therefore the lord of the vineyard do? he will come and destroy the husbandmen, and will give the vineyard unto others.* (Mark 12:9). Ezra names what the vineyard is before the parable ever has to explain it: one people gotten out of all the multitudes, loved, and given a law. The lord of the vineyard in the parable owns it because he chose it; the husbandmen only hold it. When they beat his servants and kill his heir, what he takes from them is the stewardship, and that is what he gives to others. The one people the Most High loved and gave his law to is still his vineyard; it was never the keepers' to lose.
member_note: 2 Esdras 5:27 — *among all the multitudes of people you have gotten you one people.* The lord of the vineyard at Mark 12:9 takes back the keeping of a people that was always his.

new_note: *And among all the multitudes of people you have gotten you one people: and to this people, whom you lovedst, you gavest a law that is approved of all.* (2 Esdras 5:27). *Then began he to speak to the people this parable; A certain man planted a vineyard, and let it forth to husbandmen, and went into a far country for a long time.* (Luke 20:9). The vineyard a certain man plants and lets out is the one people Ezra names, loved out of all the multitudes and given a law that is approved of all. The fruit the owner later sends his servants to collect is the fruit that law was given to bring, a people keeping what they were given. The husbandmen hold the vineyard while refusing its fruit; that is a leadership that keeps the title to the people while setting aside the law the people were planted under. The prayer and the parable agree on what the vineyard is and what it was planted for.
member_note: 2 Esdras 5:27 — *to this people, whom you lovedst, you gavest a law that is approved of all.* The vineyard let out at Luke 20:9 is this people, and the fruit sought is the law kept.

new_note: *And they which did gainsay your promises, and believed not your covenants, have trodden them down.* (2 Esdras 5:29). *What shall therefore the lord of the vineyard do? he will come and destroy the husbandmen, and will give the vineyard unto others.* (Mark 12:9). In Ezra's prayer the ones who trod the people down are the ones who gainsaid the promises and did not believe the covenants, the many nations the one people had been given over to (2 Esdras 5:28). In the parable the same unbelief shows up inside the hedge: the husbandmen entrusted with the vineyard beat the servants and kill the heir, acting as though the owner's word about returning were empty. Ezra asks why the Most High lets his people be trodden down; the parable answers with what the lord of the vineyard will do when he comes. Those who tread down what the covenants cover, whether from outside the hedge or from within it, meet the same owner.
member_note: 2 Esdras 5:29 — *they which did gainsay your promises, and believed not your covenants, have trodden them down.* The husbandmen of Mark 12:9 carry the same unbelief inside the hedge, and meet the same owner.
flag: The old note identified Ezra's 'they which did gainsay your promises' with the wicked husbandmen. In 2 Esdras 5:28–29 the ones treading the people down are the many nations the one people was given over to, not its own keepers. I kept the connection as the same unbelief seen from outside the hedge (Ezra) and from inside it (the parable), rather than making them the same men.

new_note: *And when the world, that shall begin to vanish away, shall be finished, then will I shew these tokens: the books shall be opened before the firmament, and they shall see all together:* (2 Esdras 6:20). *And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before Elohim (God); and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.* (Revelation 20:12). Ezra is told the order of the end: when this vanishing world is finished, the books are opened before the firmament and all see together. John sees the same moment from the other side of it, the dead small and great standing before Elohim (God), the books opened, and another book opened with them, the book of life. Both witnesses put the opening of the books after the world's course is run, not before it. What Ezra was told would be shown as a token, John watched being done.
member_note: 2 Esdras 6:20 — *the books shall be opened before the firmament, and they shall see all together.* John sees the same books opened before the throne at Revelation 20:12.

new_note: *And the men that are received shall see it, who have not tasted death from their birth: and the heart of the inhabitants shall be changed, and turned into another meaning.* (2 Esdras 6:26). *That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.* (Matthew 13:35). Among the tokens of the end Ezra is told that the heart of the inhabitants will be changed and turned into another meaning, and that men who have not tasted death will see it. When Yahusha (Jesus) teaches in parables he is uttering what had been kept secret from the foundation of the world, and a parable only opens to a heart that has been turned toward its meaning; to everyone else it stays a story about seed and soil. Ezra goes on to hear that the truth so long without fruit shall be declared (2 Esdras 6:28). The parables are that declaring begun, and the changed heart is the one that hears them.
member_note: 2 Esdras 6:26 — *the heart of the inhabitants shall be changed, and turned into another meaning.* The parables of Matthew 13:35 open what was kept secret to a heart turned toward their meaning.
flag: The old note quoted 2 Esdras 6:26–28 and leaned on v.28 ('the truth, which hath been so long without fruit, shall be declared'), which is not in this packet. I rebuilt on the live 6:26 (the changed heart) and mentioned v.28 in prose. The author may prefer this card to sit at 6:28.

new_note: *For my son the Messiah shall be revealed with those that be with him, and they that remain shall rejoice within four hundred years.* (2 Esdras 7:28). *And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.* (Matthew 9:27). Ezra is told that the Most High's own son, the Messiah, will be revealed, with those that are with him. Two blind men who cannot see him cry out to him on the road as the Son of David and ask for mercy. What was spoken to Ezra as something still coming, they confess as someone present. The one the Most High calls my son and the one the blind men call Son of David are the same man standing in the road.
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:28 — *my son the Messiah shall be revealed with those that be with him.* The blind men of Matthew 9:27 confess as present the one Ezra was told would be revealed.
flag: The old note carried a textual remark that the seeded text's 'Yahusha (Jesus)' at this verse was corrected to 'the Messiah'. The live text already reads 'my son the Messiah', so nothing needed fixing; I left the remark out since the reader cannot see it. The 'within four hundred years' clause is not addressed by the note.

new_note: *After these years shall my son Messiah (Christ) die, and all men that have life. And the world shall be turned into the old silence seven days, like as in the former judgments: so that no man shall remain.* (2 Esdras 7:29–30). *Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour.* (Matthew 27:45). Ezra is told that the Messiah will die, and that the world will then be turned back into the old silence, as in the former judgments, before the raising up that follows (2 Esdras 7:31–32). When Yahusha (Jesus) hung on the tree, darkness lay over all the land from the sixth hour to the ninth, as if creation had drawn back toward its first dark. The three hours were not the seven days; they were a small showing of them, the world going quiet at the death of the Messiah (Christ) before the graves gave up their dead (Matthew 27:52). Amos had said *I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day* (Amos 8:9); Ezra was told the Messiah's death brings the old silence; the cross carried both for three hours.
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:30 — *the world shall be turned into the old silence seven days.* The three hours of darkness at Matthew 27:45 were a small showing of that silence.

new_note: *And the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her, and so shall the dust those that dwell in silence, and the secret places shall deliver those souls that were committed to them.* (2 Esdras 7:32). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Ezra is shown the order: first the earth gives back those asleep in her and the secret places deliver the souls committed to them, then the Most High appears on the seat of judgment, and the work follows and the reward is shown (2 Esdras 7:33–35). Yahusha (Jesus) gives the same order in one sentence: the Son of Adam comes in his Father's glory, and then he rewards every man according to his works. Resurrection first, then the reward by works. The righteous who sleep are not being rewarded somewhere now; they rest in the places committed to them until the earth restores them, and the reckoning comes after.
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:32 — *the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her.* Resurrection first, then reward according to works, as the Son of Adam says at Matthew 16:27.

new_note: *And the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her, and so shall the dust those that dwell in silence, and the secret places shall deliver those souls that were committed to them.* (2 Esdras 7:32). *And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose,* (Matthew 27:52). Ezra is told that the earth will restore those asleep in her, that the dust will give back those that dwell in silence. At the cross the earth quaked and the graves were opened, and many bodies of the saints that slept arose. The earth was doing in small measure what Ezra was told she will do fully: giving back what was sleeping in her. The saints who came out of their graves that day are a first showing of the resurrection the fathers are still waiting for, the first resurrection in which the faithful who fell asleep are raised (Revelation 20:4–6; Hebrews 11:39–40).
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:32 — *the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her, and so shall the dust those that dwell in silence.* The graves opened and the sleeping saints arose at Matthew 27:52, a first showing of it.

new_note: *And the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her, and so shall the dust those that dwell in silence, and the secret places shall deliver those souls that were committed to them.* (2 Esdras 7:32). *And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.* (Luke 16:31). Ezra names where the dead wait: asleep in the earth, in the dust, in secret places that hold the souls committed to them until the day they are delivered. When Abraham tells the rich man that his brothers would not be persuaded even if one rose from the dead, he is speaking from inside that same expectation: the dead are held, and one coming back from among them is a thing that could happen. What the brothers have now is Moses and the prophets. If those are not heard, a voice come back from the secret places will not be heard either.
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:32 — *the secret places shall deliver those souls that were committed to them.* The one who might rise from the dead at Luke 16:31 would come from that same holding place.

new_note: *And the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her, and so shall the dust those that dwell in silence, and the secret places shall deliver those souls that were committed to them.* (2 Esdras 7:32). *Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day.* (John 11:24). Martha, grieving, says what the Hebrew library had taught her: her brother will rise again in the resurrection at the last day. Ezra was told the same thing in fuller words, that the earth will restore those asleep in her and the secret places will deliver the souls committed to them. Martha's hope is not a vague comfort; it is this promise. And the one standing in front of her is about to call Lazarus out of the grave (John 11:43–44), a first sign of the day Ezra was shown.
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:32 — *the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her.* Martha's resurrection at the last day (John 11:24) is this promise, and Lazarus is its first sign.

new_note: *And the Most High shall appear upon the seat of judgment, and misery shall pass away, and the long suffering shall have an end:* (2 Esdras 7:33). *And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;* (Matthew 27:51). In Ezra's order, once the earth has given back her dead the Most High appears upon the seat of judgment, and misery and long suffering come to an end. At the moment Yahusha (Jesus) died the veil of the temple tore from top to bottom, the earth quaked, the rocks split, and the graves were opened (Matthew 27:52). The signs that belong to the day of the Most High's appearing broke through for a moment at the cross. It was not that day, but it carried the marks of it, the way a first shaking tells of the one still to come (Haggai 2:6–7).
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:33 — *the Most High shall appear upon the seat of judgment, and misery shall pass away.* The veil rent and the earth quaking at Matthew 27:51 carry the marks of that day.

new_note: *And the work shall follow, and the reward shall be shewed, and the good deeds shall be of force, and wicked deeds shall bear no rule.* (2 Esdras 7:35). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Ezra is told what follows the judgment seat: the work follows the man, the reward is shown, and good deeds are of force while wicked deeds bear no rule. Yahusha (Jesus) says it as plainly: when the Son of Adam comes in his Father's glory, he rewards every man according to his works. This is not a man earning his place; it is a man's deeds going with him into the day and being weighed there. The works that follow are the fruit of a heart that kept what it was given, and those with no such fruit are told to depart (Matthew 7:23).
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:35 — *the work shall follow, and the reward shall be shewed.* At Matthew 16:27 the Son of Adam rewards every man according to his works.

new_note: *And the work shall follow, and the reward shall be shewed, and the good deeds shall be of force, and wicked deeds shall bear no rule.* (2 Esdras 7:35). *And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.* (Matthew 25:30). Ezra is told that at the judgment the work follows and the reward is shown, that good deeds are of force and wicked ones bear no rule. The servant in the parable was given a talent and called a servant; he belonged to the house. What condemned him was not that he was never the master's, but that his work did not follow, and so he is cast into the outer darkness. The warning here is to those inside the household whose deeds bore no fruit, which is why it is so sharp.
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:35 — *the good deeds shall be of force, and wicked deeds shall bear no rule.* The unprofitable servant of Matthew 25:30 was of the house, and his work did not follow him.

new_note: *O you Adam, what have you done? for though it was you that sinned, you are not fallen alone, but we all that come of you.* (2 Esdras 7:48). *Then goeth he, and taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first. Even so shall it be also unto this wicked generation.* (Matthew 12:45). Ezra cries out to Adam that his fall did not stay with him; everyone who comes of him fell with him, carrying the grain of evil seed sown in Adam's heart from the beginning (2 Esdras 4:30). Yahusha (Jesus) describes a house swept clean of its unclean spirit but left empty, so that the spirit returns with seven worse and the last state is worse than the first. A son of Adam cleaned out but not given a new heart is that empty house; the inherited pattern comes back to fill what was only swept. The remedy is not a cleaner house but a different heart in it (Ezekiel 36:26).
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:48 — *though it was you that sinned, you are not fallen alone, but we all that come of you.* The swept but empty house of Matthew 12:45 is a son of Adam without a new heart.

new_note: *And he answered me, saying, The most High has made this world for many, but the world to come for few.* (2 Esdras 8:1). *So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.* (Matthew 20:16). Ezra asks why so many are made for so little, and the answer is plain: this world was made for many, the world to come for few. Yahusha (Jesus) closes the parable of the labourers with the same count: many are called, few chosen. The call goes out broadly because the sheep are scattered among many and no one can tell them by sight; the few are the ones who hear and come in and bear fruit. The many and the few are not two peoples set against each other; they are the whole field and the harvest that comes out of it.
member_note: 2 Esdras 8:1 — *The most High has made this world for many, but the world to come for few.* Many called, few chosen (Matthew 20:16) is the same count.

new_note: *And he answered me, saying, The most High has made this world for many, but the world to come for few.* (2 Esdras 8:1). *And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut.* (Matthew 25:10). Ten virgins went out to meet the bridegroom, and all ten were called to the wedding; only those who were ready went in before the door was shut. That is Ezra's answer told as a story: this world is made for many, the world to come for few. The five who found the door shut were not strangers; they were virgins with lamps who had gone out to meet him. The few are those found ready when he comes, which is why readiness matters more than having once set out.
member_note: 2 Esdras 8:1 — *this world for many, but the world to come for few.* The shut door of Matthew 25:10 divides the many who set out from the few found ready.

new_note: *And he answered me, saying, The most High has made this world for many, but the world to come for few.* (2 Esdras 8:1). *Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:* (Matthew 7:13). Ezra is told that this world was made for many and the world to come for few. Yahusha (Jesus) draws the same two ways on the ground: a wide gate and a broad way crowded with the many, and a strait gate that few find (Matthew 7:14). The many of the broad way are the many of this world; the few of the narrow way are the few of the world to come. The numbers match because the two men are describing the same thing.
member_note: 2 Esdras 8:1 — *made this world for many, but the world to come for few.* The broad way and the strait gate of Matthew 7:13 carry the same many and few.

new_note: *There be many created, but few shall be saved.* (2 Esdras 8:3). *So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just,* (Matthew 13:49). Ezra is told that many are created but few saved, after the likeness of much clay and little gold (2 Esdras 8:2). Yahusha (Jesus) puts the sorting at the end of the world, when the angels sever the wicked from among the just as a net full of every kind is sorted on the shore. The net gathers all; the shore keeps few. The few saved are what remains when that severing is done.
member_note: 2 Esdras 8:3 — *There be many created, but few shall be saved.* The angels sever the wicked from among the just at Matthew 13:49; the few are what remains.

new_note: *There be many created, but few shall be saved.* (2 Esdras 8:3). *So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.* (Matthew 20:16). The angel gives Ezra the plainest form of it: many created, few saved. Yahusha (Jesus) says many called, few chosen. The few are not those who saved themselves by effort, nor a number chosen apart from how they walked; they are the ones whose names were written from the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8), who hear because they are his sheep, and whose walk bears the fruit that keeps a name from being blotted out (Revelation 3:5). Being created does not make a man one of the few, and neither does being called. Hearing and keeping do, and those come from what he already was.
member_note: 2 Esdras 8:3 — *There be many created, but few shall be saved.* Many called, few chosen (Matthew 20:16); the few are the sheep who hear and keep.

new_note: *There be many created, but few shall be saved.* (2 Esdras 8:3). *But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not.* (Matthew 25:12). Many created, few saved: Ezra receives it as the hard rule of the age. The foolish virgins knock at the shut door and hear I know you not, the same word spoken to those who say Lord, Lord and work iniquity (Matthew 7:23). They were among the called and they were not among the few. Ezra's few saved and the bridegroom's I know you not are the two ends of one sentence.
member_note: 2 Esdras 8:3 — *There be many created, but few shall be saved.* The bridegroom's I know you not at Matthew 25:12 is the other end of the same sentence.

new_note: *O Yahuah (God), if you suffer not your servant, that we may pray before you, and you give us seed to our heart, and culture to our understanding, that there may come fruit of it; how shall each man live that is corrupt, who bears the place of a man?* (2 Esdras 8:6). *Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field:* (Matthew 13:24). Ezra prays for seed to the heart and culture to the understanding, so that fruit may come, because a corrupt man cannot live any other way. The kingdom parable answers that prayer with a sower: a man goes out and sows good seed in his field. The seed to the heart Ezra begs for is what the sower is sowing; the fruit Ezra hopes for is what the good ground brings forth (Matthew 13:23). The prayer and the parable meet in the same field.
member_note: 2 Esdras 8:6 — *give us seed to our heart, and culture to our understanding, that there may come fruit of it.* The sower of Matthew 13:24 is the answer to this prayer.

new_note: *For as the husbandman sows much seed upon the ground, and planteth many trees, and yet the thing that is sown good in his season comes not up, neither does all that is planted take root: even so is it of them that are sown in the world; they shall not all be saved.* (2 Esdras 8:41). *They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away.* (Luke 8:13). Ezra is told the husbandman's experience: much seed sown, many trees planted, and not all of it comes up or takes root. Yahusha (Jesus) names the rocky ground the same way: hearers who receive the word with joy, have no root, believe for a while, and fall away when tried. Springing up is not the same as taking root. Ezra's not all saved and the parable's fall away are the same plant dying for the same reason.
member_note: 2 Esdras 8:41 — *neither does all that is planted take root.* The rock hearers of Luke 8:13 spring up with no root and fall away.

new_note: *In that you have humbled thyself, as it becometh you, and have not judged thyself worthy to be much glorified among the righteous.* (2 Esdras 8:49). *I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.* (Luke 18:14). The Most High tells Ezra that what is marvellous in him is that he humbled himself and did not judge himself worthy to be much glorified among the righteous. The publican in the temple does the same, standing afar off and asking for mercy, and he goes home justified while the one who exalted himself does not. The rule Yahusha (Jesus) states, that the humble are exalted, is the rule by which Ezra is commended. Ezra's not counting himself worthy is exactly what the Most High counts worthy.
member_note: 2 Esdras 8:49 — *have not judged thyself worthy to be much glorified among the righteous.* He that humbleth himself shall be exalted (Luke 18:14) is the rule Ezra is commended by.

new_note: *And they that have loathed my law, while they had yet liberty, and, when as yet place of repentance was open to them, understood not, but despised it;* (2 Esdras 9:11). *For John came unto you in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him: and ye, when ye had seen it, repented not afterward, that ye might believe him.* (Matthew 21:32). The Most High describes those who loathed his law while they still had liberty, while a place of repentance stood open to them, and despised it. The chief priests and elders are told the same about themselves: John came in the way of righteousness, which is the law's own way, and they did not believe him, and even after watching publicans and harlots repent they did not repent afterward. The open place of repentance was John at the Jordan; they walked past it. Ezra's lament and the King's rebuke describe the same men in the same posture.
member_note: 2 Esdras 9:11 — *when as yet place of repentance was open to them, understood not, but despised it.* The chief priests who would not repent when John came (Matthew 21:32) walked past that open place.

new_note: *Let the multitude perish then, which was born in vain; and let my grape be kept, and my plant; for with great labour have I made it perfect.* (2 Esdras 9:22). *So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.* (Matthew 20:16). The Most High tells Ezra he will let the multitude born in vain perish and keep his grape and his plant, made perfect with great labour. The parable ends the same way: many called, few chosen. The grape kept out of the cluster is the few; the great labour is the Father's long keeping of his seed through all the scattering until the gathering. He does not lose what he laboured over, and he does not keep what he never planted.
member_note: 2 Esdras 9:22 — *let my grape be kept, and my plant; for with great labour have I made it perfect.* The grape kept out of the cluster is the few chosen of Matthew 20:16.

new_note: *For, behold, I sow my law in you, and it shall bring fruit in you, and you shall be honoured in it for ever.* (2 Esdras 9:31). *And these are they which are sown on good ground; such as hear the word, and receive it, and bring forth fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixty, and some an hundred.* (Mark 4:20). The law is spoken of here as seed: I sow my law in you, and it shall bring fruit in you. The good ground in the parable is those who hear the word, receive it, and bring forth fruit, thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. The word sown in Mark is the law sown in Ezra, and the fruit is the same fruit, a people keeping what was put in them. Ezra goes on to say that the fathers who received it and kept it not perished (2 Esdras 9:32–33), which is the other soils of the parable.
member_note: 2 Esdras 9:31 — *I sow my law in you, and it shall bring fruit in you.* The good ground of Mark 4:20 brings forth the fruit the sown law was given to bring.

new_note: *For, behold, I sow my law in you, and it shall bring fruit in you, and you shall be honoured in it for ever.* (2 Esdras 9:31). *Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of Elohim (God).* (Luke 8:11). When Yahusha (Jesus) explains the parable, he says the seed is the word of Elohim (God). Ezra had already heard the Most High say what that seed is: I sow my law in you. The law is the word sown, and it is sown into the hearer to bring fruit there, not handed to him as a weight to carry. There is no gap between the word of Elohim (God) in the gospel and the law in Ezra; they are one seed.
member_note: 2 Esdras 9:31 — *I sow my law in you, and it shall bring fruit in you.* The seed is the word of Elohim (God) at Luke 8:11, and the word sown is the law.

new_note: *Yet they that received it perished, because they kept not the thing that was sown in them.* (2 Esdras 9:33). *But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience.* (Luke 8:15). Ezra says why the fathers perished: they received what was sown and did not keep it. The good ground in the parable is the opposite in every word, an honest and good heart that hears the word, keeps it, and brings forth fruit with patience. Receiving is not the dividing line; keeping is. The fruit is the keeping, and the perishing is the not keeping.
member_note: 2 Esdras 9:33 — *they that received it perished, because they kept not the thing that was sown in them.* The good ground of Luke 8:15 hears the word and keeps it; the fruit is the keeping.

new_note: *And the lion, whom you sawest rising up out of the wood, and roaring, and speaking to the eagle, and rebuking her for her unrighteousness with all the words which you have heard; This is the anointed, which the Highest has kept for them and for their wickedness to the end: he shall reprove them, and shall upbraid them with their cruelty.* (2 Esdras 12:31–32). *And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.* (Matthew 9:27). Ezra's lion comes up roaring out of the wood and rebukes the eagle, which he had been told is the fourth kingdom Daniel saw (2 Esdras 12:11), and the angel then names the lion: the anointed, kept by the Highest to the end. Two blind men on the road name the same figure by his line, Son of David. The anointed one Ezra saw as a lion, the blind men perceived with no eyes, and they cried out to him as present. The Messiah (Christ) kept for the end was walking past them.
member_note: 2 Esdras 12:31 — *the lion, whom you sawest rising up out of the wood, and roaring.* The lion named as the anointed is the Son of David the blind men cry to at Matthew 9:27.

new_note: *This is the anointed, which the Highest has kept for them and for their wickedness to the end: he shall reprove them, and shall upbraid them with their cruelty.* (2 Esdras 12:32). *And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.* (Matthew 9:27). The angel tells Ezra what the lion is: the anointed, kept by the Highest to the end, who will reprove the wicked for their cruelty. Two blind men cry to Yahusha (Jesus) as Son of David, the line the anointed king comes from. The one kept to the end to reprove the proud is the one who stops in the road for the blind who ask for mercy. The same anointed, seen by Ezra in a vision and met on a road.
member_note: 2 Esdras 12:32 — *This is the anointed, which the Highest has kept for them.* The anointed kept to the end is the Son of David met on the road at Matthew 9:27.

new_note: *For the rest of my people shall he deliver with mercy, those that have been pressed upon my borders, and he shall make them joyful until the coming of the day of judgment, of which I have spoken to you from the beginning.* (2 Esdras 12:34). *And when Yahusha (Jesus) departed thence, two blind men followed him, crying, and saying, Thou Son of David, have mercy on us.* (Matthew 9:27). The anointed does two things in Ezra's vision: he reproves the eagle, and he delivers the rest of the people with mercy, those pressed upon the borders, and makes them joyful until the day of judgment. The blind men ask the Son of David for exactly that, mercy. The remnant pressed at the borders are the scattered of Yashar'el (Israel), and the first work of the Messiah (Christ) toward them is mercy, as it was for the two who cried out. He saw the multitudes as sheep having no shepherd and was moved for them (Matthew 9:36).
member_note: 2 Esdras 12:34 — *the rest of my people shall he deliver with mercy, those that have been pressed upon my borders.* The blind men ask the Son of David for that same mercy at Matthew 9:27.

new_note: *And the time shall be when these things shall come to pass, and the signs shall happen which I shewed you before, and then shall my Son be declared, whom you sawest as a man ascending.* (2 Esdras 13:32). *And then shall appear the sign of the Son of Adam in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of Adam coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.* (Matthew 24:30). Ezra sees a man come up out of the sea and is told that when the signs have happened, the Most High's Son will be declared. Yahusha (Jesus) sets the same order on the Mount of Olives: after the tribulation the sign of the Son of Adam appears in heaven and all the tribes of the earth see him coming in the clouds with power and great glory. The signs come first, then the Son is shown openly to all. Ezra was given the sequence; Matthew names the one it is about.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:32 — *then shall my Son be declared, whom you sawest as a man ascending.* The Son of Adam seen coming in the clouds at Matthew 24:30 is the Son declared after the signs.

new_note: *And when all the people hear his voice, every man shall in their own land leave the battle they have one against another.* (2 Esdras 13:33). *My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:* (John 10:27). When the Son is declared, Ezra is told, all the people hear his voice and every man leaves his battle in his own land. Yahusha (Jesus) says his sheep hear his voice, and he knows them, and they follow him. The hearing is what shows who they are; the ones who leave their fighting when he speaks are the ones who were his. His voice does not make sheep; it calls the sheep out of the battle they were in.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:33 — *when all the people hear his voice, every man shall in their own land leave the battle.* My sheep hear my voice (John 10:27); the hearing shows who they were.

new_note: *And whereas you sawest that he gathered another peaceable multitude to him; Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.* (2 Esdras 13:39–40). *And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.* (Matthew 24:31). Ezra asks about the peaceable multitude the man from the sea gathers to himself, and the Most High tells him outright who they are: the ten tribes carried out of their own land by Salmanasar of Assyria and taken over the waters into another land. The elect gathered from the four winds at the sound of the trumpet are that multitude. The gathering Yahusha (Jesus) describes is not the assembling of whoever has decided to believe; it is the homecoming of a scattered people the Most High kept, named here by tribe. Ezra tells us whom the angels are sent to gather.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:39 — *he gathered another peaceable multitude to him.* The elect gathered from the four winds at Matthew 24:31 are the ten tribes the next verse names.

new_note: *And whereas you sawest that he gathered another peaceable multitude to him; Those are the ten tribes, which were carried away prisoners out of their own land in the time of Osea the king, whom Salmanasar the king of Assyria led away captive, and he carried them over the waters, and so came they into another land.* (2 Esdras 13:39–40). *And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven.* (Mark 13:27). The man who comes up from the sea gathers a peaceable multitude to himself, and Ezra is told in the next breath who they are: the ten tribes Salmanasar of Assyria carried away captive over the waters into another land. When Yahusha (Jesus) says the angels will gather his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth, that is the multitude he means. The elect are not a people assembled out of whoever chose to join; they are the scattered seed of Yashar'el (Israel) brought home from where they were carried. Ezra puts a name on the ones the four winds give back.
member_note: 2 Esdras 13:39 — *he gathered another peaceable multitude to him.* The elect gathered from the four winds at Mark 13:27 are the ten tribes the next verse names.
